lessons.name: What is a Monolith?
lessons.desc: A monolith is a single application where ALL the code runs in one process and deploys as one unit. Login, ordering, payments, emails — one codebase, one server, one deploy command.
lessons.q: What is a monolith? Why is it the correct starting architecture for most products?
lessons.qsub: If microservices are the solution, what exactly is the problem they solve that a monolith cannot?

lessons.name: Why Monoliths Work Well Early
lessons.desc: Monoliths are simpler in every dimension: function calls instead of network calls (microseconds vs milliseconds), one database transaction covers everything, you can read all code in one place.
lessons.q: Why are monoliths simpler than microservices? What advantages do they have in the early stages?
lessons.qsub: What is premature splitting and why is it the most common microservices mistake?

lessons.name: What Breaks at Scale
lessons.desc: Monoliths break at scale in four concrete ways: independent scaling becomes impossible, deployments become risky, teams block each other, and one crash takes down everything.
lessons.q: What are the four concrete ways a monolith breaks at scale?
lessons.qsub: Are these pain points always present, or do they only appear at a certain scale?

lessons.name: What is a Microservice?
lessons.desc: A microservice is a small, independently deployable process that owns one business domain. Each service has its OWN codebase, database, and deployment pipeline.
lessons.q: What is a microservice? How does it differ from a monolith architecturally?
lessons.qsub: When drawing service boundaries in a system design interview, what principles guide the split?

lessons.name: When NOT to Use Microservices
lessons.desc: Microservices require Docker, Kubernetes, a service registry, distributed tracing, a message broker, and engineers who know all of it. A 3-person team using microservices spends more time on infrastructure than on product.
lessons.q: When should you NOT use microservices? What is the team size test?
lessons.qsub: What is a distributed monolith and how is it worse than a regular monolith?

lessons.name: Conway's Law
lessons.desc: Organizations design systems that mirror their own communication structure. A company with 5 engineering teams will inevitably build 5 services. Amazon applied this deliberately with the two-pizza team rule.
lessons.q: What is Conway's Law and how does it influence service boundary decisions?
lessons.qsub: What is the Inverse Conway Maneuver and how did Amazon use it to shape AWS?

lessons.name: Microservices Fundamentals
lessons.desc: Architectural style where app is a collection of loosely coupled, independently deployable services. Each owns its domain, data, and lifecycle.
lessons.q: What are the core characteristics of microservices? What tradeoffs do they introduce?
lessons.qsub: How do you determine the right level of service granularity — too fine vs too coarse?

lessons.name: Decomposition Strategies
lessons.desc: Domain-driven design defines bounded contexts — each service owns a subdomain. Strangler Fig pattern for incremental migration. Vertical slicing over horizontal.
lessons.q: How do you decide where to draw service boundaries? What is a Bounded Context?
lessons.qsub: How does the Strangler Fig pattern enable gradual migration from monolith to microservices?

lessons.name: Inter-service Communication
lessons.desc: Synchronous (HTTP/gRPC) for request-response. Asynchronous (messages/events) for decoupling. gRPC uses protobuf, HTTP/2, streaming — preferred for internal service-to-service.
lessons.q: Compare synchronous and asynchronous inter-service communication. When would you use each?
lessons.qsub: What is the difference between choreography and orchestration in service communication?

lessons.name: API Gateway & BFF Pattern
lessons.desc: Single entry point for all clients — routes, aggregates, transforms. BFF (Backend For Frontend): separate gateway per client type (mobile, web, IoT).
lessons.q: What is an API Gateway and why is it necessary in a microservices architecture?
lessons.qsub: What is the BFF pattern? Why might mobile and web clients need different gateways?

lessons.name: Service Discovery
lessons.desc: How services find each other's network locations. Client-side: service registry + client load balancing. Server-side: load balancer in front (K8s Service, AWS ALB).
lessons.q: How do services discover each other in a dynamic environment like Kubernetes?
lessons.qsub: What is the difference between client-side and server-side service discovery?

lessons.name: Database per Service
lessons.desc: Each service owns its data exclusively — no direct DB sharing. Polyglot persistence: choose the right DB per service (SQL for orders, document for catalog, graph for recommendations).
lessons.q: Why must each microservice own its own database? What happens when services share a DB?
lessons.qsub: What is polyglot persistence and when would you use different database types per service?

lessons.name: Saga Pattern
lessons.desc: Sequence of local transactions with compensating rollbacks. Choreography: each service listens for events and acts. Orchestration: central coordinator tells each service what to do.
lessons.q: How do you handle a transaction that spans multiple services? Explain the Saga pattern.
lessons.qsub: What is the difference between choreography and orchestration in sagas? When do you choose each?

lessons.name: CQRS & Event Sourcing
lessons.desc: CQRS separates read models (queries) from write models (commands). Event sourcing stores all state changes as an append-only event log — current state is derived by replaying events.
lessons.q: What is CQRS and when does it make sense in a microservices architecture?
lessons.qsub: How does Event Sourcing give you an audit trail and enable temporal queries?

lessons.name: Event-driven Architecture
lessons.desc: Services communicate through events — producers emit facts, consumers react. Message brokers (Kafka, RabbitMQ) provide durability, ordering, and routing.
lessons.q: What is event-driven architecture? How does it decouple services?
lessons.qsub: Compare Kafka and RabbitMQ. When would you choose one over the other?

lessons.name: Data Consistency
lessons.desc: No distributed transactions across services. Embrace eventual consistency. CAP theorem in practice: partition tolerance is non-negotiable, choose consistency (CP) or availability (AP).
lessons.q: What is eventual consistency and how does it differ from strong consistency?
lessons.qsub: Explain the CAP theorem in the context of a real microservices system. What is PACELC?

lessons.name: Synchronous Communication
lessons.desc: Request-response over HTTP/REST or gRPC. Client waits for response. Simple, familiar, but couples availability — if downstream is down, caller is down too.
lessons.q: Compare REST and gRPC for inter-service communication. What are the tradeoffs?
lessons.qsub: What is cascading failure and how does synchronous communication enable it?

lessons.name: Asynchronous Messaging
lessons.desc: Producer sends message to broker → consumer processes later. Decouples sender and receiver in time and space. Message vs event: message has a specific consumer, event is a fact anyone can react to.
lessons.q: How does asynchronous messaging decouple services? What guarantees do brokers provide?
lessons.qsub: What is the difference between at-most-once, at-least-once, and exactly-once delivery?

lessons.name: Message Serialization & Schema Registry
lessons.desc: How services agree on data format. Protobuf (compact, typed, schema evolution), Avro (Hadoop-native, schema on read), JSON (human-readable, no schema).
lessons.q: Why is schema management important in event-driven systems? Compare JSON, Protobuf, and Avro.
lessons.qsub: What is a Schema Registry and how does it prevent breaking changes in production?

lessons.name: Distributed Transactions
lessons.desc: When a single operation spans multiple services. Two-phase commit (2PC) for short-lived ACID. Outbox pattern for reliable publishing. Saga for long-lived transactions.
lessons.q: How does the Outbox Pattern ensure reliable event publishing alongside database writes?
lessons.qsub: Compare 2PC and Saga for distributed transactions. When would you choose each?

lessons.name: GraphQL Federation
lessons.desc: Federated GraphQL: multiple services (subgraphs) each own a piece of a unified graph. Gateway (router) composes schemas and routes queries to correct subgraph.
lessons.q: What is GraphQL Federation and how does it differ from a monolithic GraphQL API?
lessons.qsub: What challenges does federation introduce — N+1 queries, schema drift, entity resolution?

lessons.name: Circuit Breaker
lessons.desc: Wraps remote call with state machine: CLOSED (normal) → OPEN (failing, fast-fail) → HALF-OPEN (test recovery). Prevents cascading failures and lets downstream recover.
lessons.q: Explain the Circuit Breaker pattern. What are its three states and when does it trip?
lessons.qsub: How does a circuit breaker prevent cascading failures in a microservices system?

lessons.name: Retry, Timeout & Backoff
lessons.desc: Retry transient failures with exponential backoff + jitter. Timeouts prevent waiting forever. Never retry on the critical path without circuit breaker.
lessons.q: How should you implement retries safely? What is exponential backoff with jitter?
lessons.qsub: What is a retry storm and how can bad retry logic DDoS your own system?

lessons.name: Bulkhead Pattern
lessons.desc: Isolate resources into pools so failure in one pool doesn't drain shared resources. Thread pool isolation (each service gets its own thread pool) or semaphore isolation (limit concurrent calls).
lessons.q: What is the Bulkhead pattern? How does it prevent one slow service from affecting others?
lessons.qsub: What is the difference between thread pool isolation and semaphore isolation?

lessons.name: Rate Limiting & Throttling
lessons.desc: Control how many requests a client can make in a window. Protects services from abuse, misconfiguration, or traffic spikes. Token bucket, leaky bucket, sliding window.
lessons.q: What are the main rate limiting algorithms? Compare token bucket and sliding window.
lessons.qsub: How would you implement distributed rate limiting across multiple API gateway instances?

lessons.name: Graceful Degradation & Fallbacks
lessons.desc: When a dependency fails, degrade the feature instead of breaking the user. Show cached data, hide the widget, serve a fallback response. Fail-open vs fail-closed.
lessons.q: What is graceful degradation? How do you decide between fail-open and fail-closed?
lessons.qsub: How does Amazon's product page handle a failing recommendations service?

lessons.name: Distributed Tracing
lessons.desc: Trace a single request across multiple services. Each request gets a traceId propagated in headers. Spans represent units of work. OpenTelemetry is the standard.
lessons.q: How does distributed tracing work? What is the role of traceId and spans?
lessons.qsub: What is the difference between head-based and tail-based sampling?

lessons.name: Centralized Logging
lessons.desc: All services send logs to a central platform (ELK, Loki, CloudWatch). Correlation IDs tie logs across services. Structured logging (JSON) for machine parsing.
lessons.q: Why is centralized logging essential in microservices? What is a correlation ID?
lessons.qsub: Compare ELK stack and Loki for log aggregation. What are the tradeoffs?

lessons.name: Metrics & Dashboards
lessons.desc: RED method: Rate (requests/sec), Errors (failed requests/sec), Duration (latency percentiles). Four golden signals: latency, traffic, errors, saturation.
lessons.q: What is the RED method? How do you use it to monitor microservice health?
lessons.qsub: What are Google's Four Golden Signals and how do they differ from RED?

lessons.name: Contract Testing
lessons.desc: Consumer-driven contract tests: consumer defines expectations, provider validates them against its API. Pact framework. Ensures compatibility without full integration tests.
lessons.q: What is contract testing and why is it preferred over full integration tests in microservices?
lessons.qsub: How does the Pact framework work? What is a Pact Broker?

lessons.name: Integration Testing
lessons.desc: Test services together with real dependencies. Testcontainers for DB/message broker in tests. WireMock for external API stubs. Focus on critical paths.
lessons.q: How do you test microservices with real dependencies? What is Testcontainers?
lessons.qsub: What is the ideal test pyramid for microservices? How many e2e tests should you write?

lessons.name: CI/CD for Microservices
lessons.desc: Monorepo (single repo, many services) vs polyrepo (repo per service). Monorepo: unified tooling, atomic cross-service changes, but harder to scale CI.
lessons.q: Compare monorepo and polyrepo strategies for microservices. What are the tradeoffs?
lessons.qsub: How does affected project detection work in a monorepo CI pipeline?

lessons.name: Container Orchestration
lessons.desc: Kubernetes: declarative deployment, auto-scaling, self-healing, service discovery, load balancing, secrets, and config management.
lessons.q: What are the core Kubernetes objects for running microservices? How does K8s enable self-healing?
lessons.qsub: What is the sidecar pattern in Kubernetes and how does a service mesh like Istio use it?

lessons.name: Blue/Green & Canary Deployments
lessons.desc: Blue/Green: two identical environments, switch traffic at once. Canary: gradually shift traffic (1% → 5% → 50% → 100%) — monitor metrics, rollback if needed.
lessons.q: Compare blue/green and canary deployment strategies. When would you choose each?
lessons.qsub: What is progressive delivery and how does Argo Rollouts automate canary analysis?

lessons.name: Configuration & Secrets Management
lessons.desc: Externalize config from code — environment-specific values, feature flags, and secrets. Tools: K8s ConfigMaps/Secrets, HashiCorp Vault, AWS Parameter Store.
lessons.q: How should you manage configuration and secrets in a microservices deployment?
lessons.qsub: What are dynamic secrets in HashiCorp Vault and why are they better than static credentials?

lessons.name: Why Microservices — monolith first, when to split, Conway's Law
lessons.desc: Start with monolith, split when team size or deployment frequency demands it. Conway's Law: system design mirrors org structure. Microservices add operational complexity (networking, data consistency, deployment). Split by business domain, not technical layer.
lessons.q: When should you move from a monolith to microservices? What are the hidden costs?
lessons.qsub: What is Conway's Law and how does it influence microservice boundaries? What is the strangler fig pattern?

lessons.name: Domain-Driven Design — bounded contexts, aggregates, ubiquitous language
lessons.desc: DDD aligns software with business domains. Bounded Context: autonomous domain with its own model. Aggregate: cluster of entities with a root (consistency boundary). Ubiquitous Language: shared vocabulary between devs and domain experts. Context Maps define inter-domain relationships.
lessons.q: What is a Bounded Context in DDD? How do you identify service boundaries?
lessons.qsub: What is the difference between an Aggregate and an Entity? How do you handle relationships between aggregates?

lessons.name: Kafka — event sourcing, CQRS, exactly-once semantics, consumer groups
lessons.desc: Kafka: distributed append-only log. Topics partitioned for parallelism. Consumer groups for load balancing. Exactly-once requires idempotent producers + transactional consumers. Event sourcing: store events, derive state. CQRS: separate read/write models.
lessons.q: How does Kafka achieve exactly-once delivery? What is the difference between at-least-once and exactly-once?
lessons.qsub: What is event sourcing and when would you use it? How do consumer groups work in Kafka?

lessons.name: Service Mesh — Istio, Envoy sidecar, mTLS, traffic management
lessons.desc: Service mesh handles cross-cutting concerns (observability, security, traffic) via sidecar proxies. Istio uses Envoy sidecars. mTLS between services automatically. Traffic management: canary deployments, circuit breaking, retries. Adds latency (~1-2ms per hop).
lessons.q: What is a service mesh? When does the overhead justify the benefits?
lessons.qsub: What is the difference between Istio and Linkerd? How does mTLS work in a service mesh?

lessons.name: Chaos Engineering — game days, fault injection, Netflix Chaos Monkey
lessons.desc: Chaos Engineering: deliberately inject failures to find weaknesses before they cause outages. Chaos Monkey kills random instances. Game days: coordinated failure scenarios. Steady state hypothesis: define expected behavior, then break things. Tools: Chaos Monkey, Litmus, Gremlin.
lessons.q: What is Chaos Engineering? How do you run a chaos experiment safely?
lessons.qsub: What is the difference between chaos engineering and penetration testing? How do you limit blast radius?

lessons.name: Event Storming — collaborative design, domain events, aggregates
lessons.desc: Event Storming is a workshop format for exploring complex domains. Participants map domain events (orange stickies) on a timeline. Commands (yellow), aggregates (blue), policies (purple), read models (green). Big Picture → Process Modeling → Software Design.
lessons.q: What is Event Storming and how do you facilitate one? What are the different types of stickies?
lessons.qsub: How does Event Storming help identify microservice boundaries? What is the difference between Big Picture and Design Level Event Storming?
